headline_marked: [[BMW delivers full-screen Spider-Man ads]] to car dashboards, despite prior pledge not to
headline: BMW delivers full-screen Spider-Man ads to car dashboards, despite prior pledge not to
summary: The in-car advertisement, part of a $309 million film promotion, appears on Control Displays of vehicles running OS 7, 8, 8.5, 9, or OS X built after July 2020.
details: BMW has begun delivering full-screen Spider-Man: Brand New Day movie advertisements to the dashboard Control Displays of customer vehicles. This move places branded third-party ads in cars their owners had already purchased, running from July 27 to August 10, 2026.

The advertisement appears as a banner at car startup, which drivers can click to play a full-screen animation with backing music and an ambient-lighting light show. It is available in over 70 markets on suitably equipped vehicles running BMW Operating System 7, 8, 8.5, 9, or OS X built after July 2020.

This deployment contradicts a December 2023 statement by Stephan Durach, BMW's connected-company senior vice president. He had explicitly stated the company would not sell in-car screen space for commercials, calling the car a private space.

BMW described the animation as part of a broader brand partnership with the film, a segment of a Sony Pictures promotional campaign valued at a record $309 million in worldwide media. The company framed it as a special surprise rather than an intrusion.

This isn't BMW's first controversial post-sale monetization effort. In 2020, they introduced a subscription for heated seats already installed in cars, a practice they reversed in 2023 after public backlash.
Critics argue this practice is akin to imposing advertising on property a buyer already owns. The Autopian drew a comparison to a mortgage company placing a billboard in a homeowner's yard.

headline_marked: [[On-premise RAG]] built without GPU, cloud, or Docker: 5 lessons learned
headline: On-premise RAG built without GPU, cloud, or Docker: 5 lessons learned
summary: Building RAG for public sector health systems requires overcoming common assumptions about GPUs and cloud APIs. This open-source stack runs entirely on-premise, CPU-only, with no Docker.
details: Most RAG tutorials assume GPU access and cloud APIs, but many environments, especially in public sector health, lack both. Data must stay on-network, and hardware is often CPU-only Windows Server, without Docker.

A new open-source RAG stack (github.com/psychohub/rag-onpremise) was built to run entirely on-premise. It uses ASP.NET Core 9, Ollama for local inference, Qdrant for vectors, Python for ingest, Mistral 7B LLM, and nomic-embed-text for embeddings.

Lesson one: The official Qdrant .NET SDK failed due to network proxies downgrading HTTP/2 gRPC connections to HTTP/1.1. This caused subtle connection drops and misleading error messages that took a day to diagnose.

The solution was to bypass the SDK and use HttpClient to talk directly to Qdrant's REST API. This trades some type safety for robust deployment in environments with unpredictable HTTP/2 support across network hops.

Lesson two: HttpClient's default 100-second timeout is insufficient for CPU-bound LLM inference. Mistral 7B on a modest server (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM) can take 60-120 seconds to generate a full response, leading to client timeouts.

The fix involves measuring worst-case inference times on target hardware and setting client timeouts comfortably above that. Implementing a progress indicator in the UI is also crucial to manage user expectations during long waits.
Lesson three: Ollama defaults to binding on 127.0.0.1:11434, making it inaccessible from other machines or service accounts. This causes generic connection errors, masking the actual binding issue.

To resolve this, set the OLLAMA_HOST environment variable to 0.0.0.0. When deploying Ollama as a Windows service, this variable must be set at the service level, not just in a user's PowerShell session.
caption:
Building RAG without GPU, cloud, or Docker is possible, but comes with hidden challenges. Learn 5 crucial lessons from a real-world, on-premise implementation.

Lesson one: The official Qdrant .NET SDK failed due to network proxies downgrading HTTP/2 gRPC connections to HTTP/1.1. This caused subtle connection drops and misleading error messages that took a day to diagnose.

The solution was to bypass the SDK and use HttpClient to talk directly to Qdrant's REST API. This trades some type safety for robust deployment in environments with unpredictable HTTP/2 support across network hops.

Lesson two: HttpClient's default 100-second timeout is insufficient for CPU-bound LLM inference. Mistral 7B on a modest server (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM) can take 60-120 seconds to generate a full response, leading to client timeouts.

To resolve this, set the OLLAMA_HOST environment variable to 0.0.0.0. When deploying Ollama as a Windows service, this variable must be set at the service level, not just in a user's PowerShell session.
